text: Some servers, by the nature of their job, have to be reachable from the public internet — a company website, a public mail server, a customer-facing API. Anything reachable from the internet is also reachable by an attacker, and a public-facing server is realistically the most likely thing on the network to eventually get compromised. The real question isn't whether it might be breached, but what happens to the rest of the network if it is.

A DMZ, or demilitarized zone, is a separate network segment sitting between the internet and the internal network, used specifically to host public-facing servers. Traffic from the internet can reach the DMZ, and the DMZ can reach specific internal resources under tightly controlled conditions, but the internet never gets a direct path into the internal network, and a breach of a DMZ host doesn't hand an attacker a direct line into it either.

A company's public website runs on a server placed in the DMZ, reachable from the internet on port 80 or 443. If that web server is compromised, the attacker lands inside the DMZ, not inside the internal network where finance servers and employee workstations live. Getting any further means getting past another firewall boundary entirely, which is exactly the delay and detection opportunity the DMZ is designed to create.

A three-legged DMZ uses one firewall with three interfaces — internet, DMZ, and internal — enforcing separate rules for each zone. It's simpler to deploy, but that single firewall is the only thing standing between the internet and the internal network. A back-to-back DMZ uses two separate firewalls with the DMZ sandwiched between them, so traffic has to clear two independent hops, often from different vendors, before reaching the internal network.

That second firewall in a back-to-back design adds real defense in depth — a flaw in one firewall doesn't automatically compromise the whole boundary — at the cost of more hardware to buy and maintain. Next up: VLANs and network segmentation strategy, extending this same idea of isolation to servers, workstations, guest Wi-Fi, and IoT devices sharing one physical network.
